summary: Describes MOBIKE, a mobility and multihoming extension to IKEv2 that allows the IP addresses of IKEv2 and tunnel-mode IPsec security associations to change. For example, a mobile VPN client could keep its connection to the VPN gateway while moving between networks. It is a standards-track protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: You are on a video call and walk from your home Wi-Fi to the street. MOBIKE lets your secure tunnel keep going even though your address changed.

questions: how to keep vpn connection when ip changes
how does mobike update ipsec addresses
subtitle: How a VPN tunnel can keep running when either end changes its IP address, without starting over.

tldr.problem: In base IKEv2 the tunnel addresses of the IKE and IPsec security associations are fixed when the IKE_SA is created, so a host that moves or loses an interface has to rebuild everything.
tldr.mechanism: MOBIKE adds a few IKEv2 notifications so the party that started the IKE_SA can announce extra addresses and ask the peer to switch the tunnel to a new address pair, with optional checks that the new address really works.
tldr.outcome: A mobile VPN client or multihomed host can move between networks while keeping its existing security associations. Only one address pair is used at a time, and both ends moving at once is not supported.

facts.label: Port after MOBIKE and NAT Traversal

today: RFC 4555 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies MOBIKE as an extension to IKEv2 as defined in RFC 4306.

sections.title: Why Tunnel Addresses Need to Change
sections.content:
IKEv2 authenticates two peers and sets up IPsec security associations (SAs). In base IKEv2 the IKE_SA and the tunnel mode IPsec SAs are tied to the IP addresses in use when the IKE_SA was created, and those addresses cannot be changed afterwards.

That is a problem when a host moves and gets a new address, or when a multihomed host wants to switch interfaces because one stopped working. Creating new SAs works but can be costly: it may need user interaction such as entering a token code, and it involves expensive calculations and possibly many round trips.

The main scenario is a remote access VPN user going from office Ethernet to a wireless LAN, then to GPRS, then to a home wireless LAN. MOBIKE updates only the outer (tunnel header) addresses. The addresses and traffic selectors inside the tunnel stay the same, so mobility is mostly invisible to applications.

Scope limits: only tunnel mode is covered, only one address pair is used for an SA at a time (no load balancing), and there is no rendezvous mechanism, so MOBIKE suits cases where at least one endpoint has a fairly stable address. It does not work over address pairs that give only one-way connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally your secure tunnel is glued to the address you started with. If you move, the glue breaks. MOBIKE lets you move the tunnel without building a new one.

sections.title: Who Decides and the Basic Idea
sections.content:
Each side may have several addresses, so there are up to N*M possible address pairs. MOBIKE keeps the decision simple: the party that started the IKE_SA (the initiator, the client in a remote access VPN) chooses which pair the IPsec SAs use, and works out which pairs work. The responder (the gateway) just tells the initiator what addresses it has and does not update the IPsec SAs until the initiator asks.

How the initiator gathers information and picks a path is largely outside MOBIKE. The protocol only covers what is visible in IKEv2 and IPsec messages.

Two features address security. A return routability check verifies that the peer can really receive packets at the address it claims, which makes it harder to flood a third party. A NAT prohibition feature detects address changes made by NATs or translators, and is used only when NAT Traversal is not in use.

NATs add limits. MOBIKE assumes that if a NAT is present, the initiator is the party behind it. Changes of the responder's address are not fully supported in that case, though the responder still tries to tell the initiator.
sections.plainLanguage: The visitor who is moving around, not the host, decides which door to use. The host just says which doors it has and waits to be told.

sections.title: Switching Addresses Step by Step
sections.content:
Support is signaled with a MOBIKE_SUPPORTED notification in the IKE_AUTH exchange. In the same exchange either side MAY list extra addresses with ADDITIONAL_IP4_ADDRESS and ADDITIONAL_IP6_ADDRESS notifications. The recipient just stores them. If MOBIKE and NAT Traversal are both supported, the peers move to port 4500 even when no NAT was seen, so ports need not change later.

When the initiator decides to change addresses (for example because requests keep being retransmitted without a valid reply), it updates the IKE_SA, then sends an INFORMATIONAL request containing UPDATE_SA_ADDRESSES from the new address. Information from lower layers can be unreliable, so it SHOULD be treated as a hint and the initiator SHOULD trigger Dead Peer Detection.

The responder takes the new addresses from the IP header of that request, checks them against local policy (replying UNACCEPTABLE_ADDRESSES if they are not acceptable), replies, optionally runs a return routability check, and then updates the IPsec SAs. The responder never updates IPsec SAs on its own, with one exception: if its current source address becomes unavailable it may switch to another.

Address lists are replaced as a whole. There are no separate add or delete operations: the full list is sent each time, or NO_ADDITIONAL_ADDRESSES if there are no other addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: When you move, you send your friend a note from your new house saying 'write to me here now'. Your friend checks the note is real and then starts using the new address.

sections.title: Checking Addresses, NATs and Paths
sections.content:
The return routability check SHOULD be done by default, normally before the IPsec SAs are updated. It can be skipped in places where the peer is expected to behave well, such as many corporate VPNs. It uses a COOKIE2 notification: the sender of an INFORMATIONAL request puts in unpredictable data of 8 to 64 octets, and the recipient MUST copy it into the response. If the values do not match, the IKE_SA MUST be closed.

When NAT Traversal is in use, NAT detection notifications can be added to ordinary INFORMATIONAL messages (such as Dead Peer Detection) to notice that a NAT mapping changed. If the destination hash differs from the earlier value, the initiator SHOULD send UPDATE_SA_ADDRESSES.

When NAT Traversal is not enabled, messages that can change addresses MUST carry a NO_NATS_ALLOWED notification holding the addresses and ports the sender used. The responder MUST compare them with the IP header and answer UNEXPECTED_NAT_DETECTED if they differ, so modification by NATs or translators is detected.

Plain Dead Peer Detection says only whether the current path works. With several addresses, the initiator can use normal INFORMATIONAL exchanges to test other paths. Because the initiator does the recovery, the responder SHOULD use long timeouts; the RFC suggests retransmitting requests for at least five minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trusting a new address, you send a secret number to it and ask for it back. Only the real person at that address can answer correctly.

sections.title: The New Notify Payloads
sections.content:
MOBIKE defines new IKEv2 Notify payload types. Two are error types: UNACCEPTABLE_ADDRESSES (40) and UNEXPECTED_NAT_DETECTED (41). The rest are status types in the 16396 to 16402 range.

For all of them the Protocol ID and SPI Size fields are zero. MOBIKE_SUPPORTED carries empty data, which is ignored on receipt so future versions can use it. The additional address notifications carry a four-octet IPv4 address or a 16-octet IPv6 address. NO_NATS_ALLOWED carries source and destination addresses and ports: 12 octets for IPv4 and 36 octets for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: These are little labeled notes the two sides pass to each other, such as 'I can do this', 'here is another address' or 'please switch now'.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MOBIKE address updates travel inside the IKE_SA, so they are encrypted, integrity protected and replay protected. But the actual addresses in the IP header are not covered, so a NAT or an on-path attacker can alter them. The RFC says the effect is limited mainly to denial of service, because traffic is still protected by IPsec.

Redirecting traffic could also be used to flood a third party. The return routability test limits how long such an attack by an off-path attacker can last, since only someone holding the IKE_SA keys who saw the request can answer it.

Policy needs care: an SA created for one place may later be used from another, so access rules based on the peer's outer address, and traffic selector authorization in particular, must account for that. Attackers may also spoof lower-layer signals, such as link errors, to push traffic elsewhere. MOBIKE offers no protection for those signals itself.

Finally, address lists reveal which networks a host is attached to, and so can reveal more about location. They are sent encrypted, and a peer need not disclose addresses it does not want to use.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes are locked so strangers cannot change them, and the secret-number test stops someone from tricking you into sending your mail to an innocent neighbor.

items.label: UNACCEPTABLE_ADDRESSES
items.desc: Address change was not carried out.

items.label: UNEXPECTED_NAT_DETECTED
items.desc: NO_NATS_ALLOWED contents did not match the IP header.

items.label: NO_ADDITIONAL_ADDRESSES
items.desc: No addresses beyond the one in use.

items.label: UPDATE_SA_ADDRESSES
items.desc: Initiator asks to switch the SAs to new addresses.

items.label: NO_NATS_ALLOWED
items.desc: Addresses and ports used, to detect NAT changes.
